title: Gaṇeśa in Gupta, Pāla and Cōḻa art (with the textual prescriptions)
subject: deity:ganesha
question: How is Gaṇeśa represented — arms, attributes, mount, posture and setting — in the Gupta, Pāla and Cōḻa traditions, and what do the texts prescribe?

rows.statement: Earliest securely datable images (4th–6th c.): two-armed, pot-bellied, without a mount; often holding his broken tusk and a bowl of sweets that the trunk reaches into; appears as an attendant figure (e.g. beside the Mothers) rather than as a main temple icon.

Eastern Indian steles (8th–12th c.): usually four-armed or more, often dancing (Nṛtta-Gaṇapati) on a lotus base with the rat below, framed by a carved back-slab with flying attendants; attributes include tusk, rosary, axe and sweets.

Tamil images (10th–13th c.) in bronze and stone: four-armed, seated or standing, goad and noose in the rear hands, tusk and modaka in the front; placed in the south niche of the main vimāna beside Dakṣiṇāmūrti in the Cōḻa programme.

Prescribes a human-bodied, big-bellied, elephant-faced Vināyaka with a sacred thread and a long trunk, holding his own tusk and an axe on one side and a laḍḍuka and a lotus on the other; gives the trunk 36 aṅgulas.
Only Kern’s text has a verse on Gaṇeśa (58.58): lord of the pramathas, elephant-faced, pendulous belly, holding an axe, single-tusked, carrying a radish; Tripathi’s text and Utpala lack it.

note: Rows are period styles, not single objects; each statement summarises typical features. The Pāla and Cōḻa rows are from recall and should be checked against specific museum objects.

title: Dancing Śiva at Bādāmi Cave 1 and in Cōḻa bronzes
subject: deity:nataraja
question: How does the earliest dated dancing Śiva of the Deccan differ from the classic Cōḻa Naṭarāja?

rows.statement: Late 6th-century rock-cut relief on the façade of Cave 1: Śiva dances with eighteen arms fanned out like a wheel, several holding a drum, trident, serpent and other attributes, many simply in dance gestures; Nandin and Gaṇeśa accompany him. There is no ring of fire and no dwarf under his foot.
Mid-6th-century Naṭarāja panel in Cave 1: an eight-armed dancing Śiva surrounded by gods, part of a programme of Śaiva panels.

11th-century bronze: four arms — upper right drum, upper left fire, lower right abhaya, lower left across the body in the elephant-trunk gesture pointing to the raised left foot; right foot on the dwarf Apasmāra; flying locks with the tiny Gaṅgā; encircled by a flaming arch (prabhāmaṇḍala/tiruvāci). This ānanda-tāṇḍava type is associated with Chidambaram.
c. 1010: Śiva is carved dancing the karaṇas of the Nāṭyaśāstra in the upper passage of the vimāna, a different, textual approach to the dancing god from the single cult bronze.

note: The Bādāmi relief is a many-armed tāṇḍava; the Cōḻa four-armed form is not derived from it in a straight line.

title: Mahiṣāsuramardinī: Kuṣāṇa, Gupta, Pallava, Pāla and the Agni Purāṇa
subject: deity:mahishasuramardini
question: How are the Goddess and the buffalo demon shown at different periods, and how does that compare with the textual prescription?

rows.statement: Kuṣāṇa Mathurā (1st–2nd c.): a small four- or six-armed goddess, standing, pressing down or lifting an entirely animal buffalo with her hands; no lion and no battle.
Early 5th c.: the Goddess, with more arms and weapons, stands over the animal buffalo, piercing it with a trident; still a static cult image.
Mid–late 7th c.: a narrative battle relief: the eight-armed Goddess rides her lion with an army of gaṇas against a buffalo-headed warrior who retreats with his troops.
Eastern India (9th–12th c.): ten- or more-armed Goddess on the lion; the demon in human form emerges from the neck of the decapitated buffalo and is held by his hair or the noose.
Caṇḍī has twenty arms (or ten); a man springs, weapon raised, from the buffalo’s neck, bound by the noose and attacked by the lion — the composition of the later images.
The narrative: Mahiṣa changes form — buffalo, lion, man, elephant — and is killed as he half-emerges from the buffalo’s mouth, pinned under the Goddess’s foot and beheaded.

note: The “emerging man” motif appears in images only after the narrative of the Devī Māhātmya was in circulation; the Kuṣāṇa images predate the surviving text.

title: The image of Viṣṇu in the Bṛhat Saṃhitā, the Agni Purāṇa, the Viṣṇudharmottara and the Mayamata
subject: deity:vishnu
question: What arms, attributes and proportions do the treatises prescribe for an image of Viṣṇu?

rows.statement: Viṣṇu may have eight, four or two arms; dark as the flax flower, in yellow garments, with Śrīvatsa and Kaustubha, crown and earrings. Eight-armed: right hands sword, mace, arrow and a peace-giving hand; left hands bow, shield, discus and conch. Four-armed: right peace-giving and mace; left conch and discus. Two-armed: right peace-giving, left conch. The image is twice the height of its pedestal, which is a third of the door height less an eighth.

The eight-armed Viṣṇu sits on Tārkṣya (Garuḍa): right hands sword, mace, arrow and varada; left hands bow, shield, discus and conch — the Bṛhat Saṃhitā’s list, but with a boon-giving instead of a peace-giving hand and with Garuḍa as mount.
The four-armed standing Viṣṇu takes twenty-four names according to the order of lotus, conch, discus and mace in the four hands (Keśava: lotus, conch, discus, mace).
The Viṣṇudharmottara gives Viṣṇu (as Vāsudeva) four arms with personified mace and discus beneath the lower hands and treats the four faces of the Vaikuṇṭha form theologically.

Southern practice: standing Viṣṇu with discus and conch in the rear hands, the front hands in abhaya/varada or resting on hip or thigh; the principal image measured on the large ten-tāla canon (uttama daśatāla).

note: The two verified Sanskrit prescriptions (BS and AP) agree almost word for word on the eight-armed Viṣṇu; the Mayamata and Viṣṇudharmottara rows are from recall and need chapter-level checking.

title: The mount of Varuṇa: goose or makara?
subject: deity:varuna
question: On what animal does Varuṇa ride?

rows.statement: Varuṇa rides a goose (haṃsa) and holds a noose.
Varuṇa rides a makara and holds a noose.

note: Medieval temple images generally follow the makara tradition.

title: The image of Sūrya: texts and early images
subject: deity:surya
question: How is the Sun god to be dressed and equipped?

rows.statement: Northern dress, covered from the feet to the chest; crown, earrings, long necklace, girdle, coat (kañcuka), jewelled halo; a lotus in each hand; nose, forehead, shanks, thighs, cheeks and chest prominent.
On a one-wheeled chariot with seven horses, holding two lotuses; Daṇḍin and Piṅgala at the door; alternatively a single Sūrya on horseback.
Kuṣāṇa Mathurā Sūryas (2nd c.): seated in a chariot drawn by two or four horses, wearing a tunic and boots, holding a lotus bud and a short sword.
13th c.: the whole temple is Sūrya’s chariot with 24 wheels and seven horses; standing booted Sūrya images in the niches.

title: The divisions of the liṅga
subject: deity:linga
question: How is the liṅga divided and proportioned?

rows.statement: Divide the length in three: square at the base, octagonal in the middle, round above; the square part is set in the ground, the middle in the pedestal; a thin, over-long liṅga ruins the land.
The three parts are assigned to Brahmā, Viṣṇu and Śiva; the octagonal part is Viṣṇu’s. Liṅgas are ranked by material, from salt, ghee and cloth through clay, wood and stone to pearl, metals and gems.

title: Who are the Mothers? Bṛhat Saṃhitā, Devī Māhātmya and Agni Purāṇa
subject: deity:matrikas
question: Which Mothers are named, and how are they distinguished?

rows.statement: Gives no list: the band of Mothers is to be made with the marks of the gods whose names they bear.

Seven śaktis come out of the gods with their forms, ornaments and mounts: Brahmāṇī (swan-car, rosary, water-pot), Māheśvarī (bull, trident), Kaumārī (peacock, spear), Vaiṣṇavī (Garuḍa, conch, discus, mace, bow, sword), Vārāhī (boar form), Nārasiṃhī (lion form) and Aindrī (elephant, thunderbolt); Śivadūtī and Cāmuṇḍā fight beside them.

Seven Mothers: four-faced Brāhmī on a swan with rosary; white Śāṅkarī on a bull; red, two-armed Kaumārī on a peacock with a spear; Vaiṣṇavī (called Lakṣmī) with discus, conch, mace and lotus; Vārāhī on a buffalo; thousand-eyed Aindrī with thunderbolt; and emaciated Cāmuṇḍā on a corpse. Nārasiṃhī is absent.

note: The Agni Purāṇa list matches the usual sculptural Saptamātṛkā row (ending with Cāmuṇḍā); the Devī Māhātmya’s seven include Nārasiṃhī instead.
